units.title: Limits, partial and directional derivatives, and gradients
outcomes: Compute partial and directional derivatives from the limit definition and evaluate them at a point by hand.
Explain the gradient as the steepest-ascent direction and relate every directional derivative to it through \(D_u f = \operatorname{grad} f \cdot u\).
Convert between row-vector (MML) and column-vector (18.S096) gradient conventions without dropping a transpose.
units.why: Every later gradient is a stack of directional derivatives. If you cannot compute one by hand and check it numerically, no backward pass output will mean anything to you.

next.note: Gradients stack into Jacobian rows and Hessian entries.
Reverse accumulation computes these partials on a graph; check it against centered differences.

study.title: Univariate derivatives, partials and gradients
study.locator: Section 5.1, Differentiation of Univariate Functions (pp. 141-145): difference quotient (5.3), derivative as a limit (5.4), polynomial derivation (5.5)-(5.6), product, quotient, sum and chain rules (5.29)-(5.32). Section 5.2, Partial Differentiation and Gradients (pp. 146-149): partial derivatives, gradient as a row vector, the chain rule as matrix multiplication (5.48)-(5.53)

study.title: Derivatives as linear operators
study.locator: Lecture 1, Part 2 notes (course notes Chapter 2, Sections 2.1-2.3): \(df = f'(x)[dx]\) as a linear operator, scalar-valued case \(df = (\operatorname{grad} f) \cdot dx\) with the gradient as the transpose of the derivative

study.title: Gradient geometry and directional derivatives
study.locator: Sessions 35 to 38 (Part B): gradient definition and perpendicularity to level curves, the proof, a worked example, directional derivatives
study.depth: Refresher only. Open only if partial derivatives or gradients are weak; it does not replace the MML derivations.

focus: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient; each partial derivative holds all other variables constant.
For unit \(u\), \(D_u f = \operatorname{grad} f \cdot u\), and the maximum over \(u\) is \(\|\operatorname{grad} f\|\) at \(u = \operatorname{grad} f / \|\operatorname{grad} f\|\) by Cauchy-Schwarz.
MML writes gradients as row vectors and 18.S096 as column vectors; the two differ by a transpose and the chain rule changes shape with the choice.
Existing partials do not imply differentiability; continuous partials do.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, differentiate \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 x_2 + x_1 x_2^3\) at (1, 2) to get \(\operatorname{grad} f = (12, 13)\), then the directional derivative along \(u = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}\), which is \(25/\sqrt{2}\) = 17.67766953. Check with float64 NumPy centered differences at \(h = 10^{-5}\): both components agree within 3e-10 absolute (measured 1.0e-11 and 2.2e-10).
traps: Reading \(D_u f\) as a partial derivative. A partial fixes an axis; a directional derivative moves along \(u\) and needs the full gradient dot product.

Assuming equal partials imply a smooth function. With \(f(x, y) = x^2 y/(x^4 + y^2)\) off the origin and \(f(0, 0) = 0\), both partials at the origin are 0, yet \(f\) equals 1/2 along \(y = x^2\), so \(f\) is discontinuous and not differentiable there.
Mixing gradient conventions across sources and silently dropping a transpose, which flips every later matrix shape.

selfTest.q: State the difference quotient and the assumption that turns it into the derivative.
selfTest.a: \((f(x + h) - f(x))/h\). The two-sided limit as \(h \to 0\) must exist. Uses: \(f\) is defined near \(x\) for the quotient, and differentiability at \(x\) for the limit.

selfTest.q: For \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 x_2 + x_1 x_2^3\), give \(\operatorname{grad} f\) at (1, 2) and \(D_u f\) for \(u = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}\).
selfTest.a: Partial derivatives are \(2 x_1 x_2 + x_2^3\) and \(x_1^2 + 3 x_1 x_2^2\), so \(\operatorname{grad} f = (12, 13)\) and \(D_u f = (12 + 13)/\sqrt{2} = 25/\sqrt{2}\) = 17.67766953.

selfTest.q: Give a function with both partials zero at the origin that is not differentiable there, and the curve that exposes it.
selfTest.a: \(f(x, y) = x^2 y/(x^4 + y^2)\) with \(f(0, 0) = 0\). Both partials at the origin are 0, but along \(y = x^2\) the value is constantly 1/2, so \(f\) is discontinuous and hence not differentiable at the origin.

selfTest.q: MML gives a \(1 \times 2\) gradient where 18.S096 gives \(2 \times 1\) for the same \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\). Which is right?
selfTest.a: Both, by stated convention. MML uses numerator layout (row); 18.S096 uses column gradients with \(df = (\operatorname{grad} f)^\top dx\). Convert with a transpose and never mix the two inside one derivation.

practice.name: MML Chapter 5, Exercise 5.5 (partial derivatives and Jacobians)
practice.locator: Exercises (pp. 170-171), Exercise 5.5: dimensions of each partial derivative in part (a), then the Jacobians in part (b)
practice.note: Do part (a) before part (b); the predicted dimensions fix the Jacobian shapes.

practice.name: TrenTorch: Directional derivatives
practice.locator: Implement directional_derivative(f, x, direction) as a centered difference along the normalized direction, and steepest_ascent_direction(f, x) as the unit gradient
practice.note: Then run both on the Reproduce cubic at (1, 2): the derivative along (1, 1) must land within 1e-9 of 17.67766953, and the steepest-ascent value must equal \(\|\operatorname{grad} f\| = \sqrt{313}\) = 17.69180601.

units.title: Jacobians, Hessians and Taylor approximations
outcomes: Assemble the Jacobian of a vector-valued map with consistent shapes under a stated layout.
Write first- and second-order Taylor approximations and bound the remainder from the Hessian size.
Classify a stationary point from Hessian eigenvalues on a small hand-worked example.
units.why: Jacobians say how outputs move; Hessians say how gradients move. Taylor turns both into the local models that justify gradient steps and Newton steps.

next.note: Hessian definiteness becomes the second-order optimality condition.
The Hessian returns as Hessian-vector products computed without forming the matrix.

study.title: Jacobians, Hessians and multivariate Taylor
study.locator: Section 5.3 (pp. 149-154): vector-valued gradients, the Jacobian, the determinant-as-magnifier example, gradient of \(f(x) = Ax\) in (5.67)-(5.68). Section 5.7 (pp. 164-165): higher-order derivatives and Hessian symmetry for twice continuously differentiable functions. Section 5.8 (pp. 165-169): multivariate Taylor series (5.149)-(5.156) with the worked cubic \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 2xy + y^3\) at (1, 2): gradient (5.165), Hessian (5.171) and third derivatives (5.174)-(5.176)

study.title: Second derivatives, bilinear forms and Hessians
study.locator: Lecture 7, Part 2 notes (course notes Chapter 12): second derivatives as symmetric bilinear forms, Hessian matrices, minima versus maxima versus saddles

study.title: Second-derivative test in two variables
study.locator: Session 30 (Part A): second-derivative test for two-variable functions
study.depth: Use only as the 2-D classification check; skip the Lagrange sessions.

focus: The Jacobian of \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is \(m \times n\) in numerator layout, and each row is one scalar gradient.
Hessian symmetry needs continuous second partials. Without \(C^2\), mixed partials can disagree and the Taylor form breaks.
The first-order remainder scales with the squared step times the Hessian size; the second-order remainder with the cubed step.
Eigenvalue signs classify: all positive is a strict local minimum, mixed signs a saddle, a zero eigenvalue leaves the test silent.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, give the Hessian \(H = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) of \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 + x_1 x_2 + x_2^2\), its eigenvalues 1 and 3 from numpy.linalg.eigvalsh, and classify the origin as a strict local minimum since \(H\) is positive definite. Verify the second-order Taylor model is exact: \(f(0.3, -0.2) = 0.07\), and \(0.5 d^\top H d\) in float64 gives 0.06999999999999999, one ulp (1.4e-17) below.
traps: Calling a stationary point with positive diagonal Hessian entries a minimum. Off-diagonals matter; only definiteness decides.
Trusting a Taylor model far from the base point. The remainder grows with powers of the step, so recompute rather than extrapolate.
Switching gradient layout mid-derivation. The layout fixes the Jacobian and Hessian shapes, so a silent switch transposes everything.

selfTest.q: For \(f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2\), what is the Jacobian shape and what is its first row?
selfTest.a: \(2 \times 3\) in numerator layout. The first row is the (row) gradient of \(f_1\).

selfTest.q: Where is the \(C^2\) assumption used in the claim that the Hessian is symmetric?
selfTest.a: Continuity of the mixed second partials lets the two differentiation orders agree. The proof step equating the two mixed partials uses exactly this continuity.

selfTest.q: Approximate \(e^{0.1}\) with \(T_1\) about 0. Give the value, the remainder and a bound.
selfTest.a: \(T_1 = 1.1\), actual value 1.10517092, remainder 0.00517092. With \(M = e^{0.1}\) bounding the second derivative on [0, 0.1], \(M h^2/2 = 0.00552585\), and the remainder satisfies the bound.

selfTest.q: Classify the stationary point with Hessian \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\).
selfTest.a: Eigenvalues 1 and 3, both positive, so the Hessian is positive definite and the point is a strict local minimum.

practice.name: TrenTorch: Hessian
practice.locator: Implement hessian(f, x) as the centered-difference Jacobian of the provided gradient, and classify_critical_point(H) from eigvalsh signs with a tolerance
practice.note: Its tests call diag(1e-9, 2) a saddle, but a near-zero eigenvalue leaves the second-derivative test silent: \(x^4 + y^2\) has Hessian diag(0, 2) at its minimum. Pass the tests, then return a fourth label for that case in your own copy.

units.title: The chain rule and matrix derivatives
outcomes: Differentiate composite scalar, vector and matrix functions with differentials and the operator chain rule.
Derive \(d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1} dX X^{-1}\) and gradients of affine, quadratic and trace objectives with correct shapes.
Predict Jacobian accumulation cost for a chain of maps and choose left-to-right versus right-to-left order.
units.why: Matrix backprop is the chain rule with shapes. Differentials keep the product order that index notation hides, and that order decides the flop count.

next.note: Loss gradients apply these differentials to least squares, logistic and softmax objectives.
The scalar engine mechanizes this chain rule with topological backward; check it against centered differences.

study.title: Operator chain rule and the inverse differential
study.locator: Lecture 1, Part 2 notes (course notes Chapter 2, Sections 2.4-2.6): operator sum, product and chain rules, \(d(A^3) = A^2 dA + A dA A + dA A^2\), \(d(A^{-1}) = -A^{-1} dA A^{-1}\), forward versus reverse Jacobian accumulation

study.title: Jacobians of matrix functions
study.locator: Lecture 2, Part 2 notes (course notes Chapter 3): the Jacobian of a matrix function via \(\operatorname{vec}\), the \(4 \times 4\) Jacobian of matrix squaring, the identity \((A \otimes B) \operatorname{vec}(C) = \operatorname{vec}(BCA^\top)\), and why forming Kronecker Jacobians costs \(m^4\) (Section 3.3.3)
study.depth: Read for the vec picture only; compute gradients with the Frobenius route in the next item.

study.title: Gradients in general vector spaces
study.locator: Lecture 4, Part 1 notes (course notes Section 5.1): the Frobenius inner product \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top B)\), gradients of matrix-input functions read off \(df = \operatorname{tr}(G^\top dA)\), with the Frobenius-norm and \(x^\top Ay\) (gradient \(xy^\top\)) examples

study.title: Matrix gradients and gradient identities
study.locator: Sections 5.2.2 and 5.4-5.5 (pp. 148-149, 155-158): chain rule as matrix multiplication, gradients of matrices, identities (5.99)-(5.108) covering transpose, trace, determinant, inverse, \(a^\top Xb\) and \(x^\top Bx\)

study.title: Derivative of the determinant and inverse
study.locator: Lecture 5, Part 1 (course notes Chapter 7): derivative of the matrix determinant and inverse, including \(d \log \det X = \operatorname{tr}(X^{-1} dX)\)

focus: \(d(fg) = (df)g + f(dg)\) keeps factor order. Matrices do not commute, so \(d(A^3)\) has three distinct terms.
\(d(X^{-1})\) comes from differentiating the constant \(XX^{-1} = I\); the final left-multiplication by \(X^{-1}\) needs \(X\) to be invertible.
Read gradients off differentials with the Frobenius product: \(df = \operatorname{tr}(G^\top dX)\) means \(\operatorname{grad} f = G\).
For three or more composed maps, accumulate Jacobians from the small side. Scalar-output chains go left to right.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1} dX X^{-1}\) from \(d(XX^{-1}) = 0\). Check in float64 NumPy with \(X = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right], V = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.5&-0.25\\0.25&0.5\end{smallmatrix}\right], h = 10^{-5}\): \(\|(X + hV)^{-1} - (X^{-1} - h X^{-1} V X^{-1})\|_F\) = 9.3e-12, a scaled residual of 0.093, consistent with an \(O(h^2)\) remainder.
traps: Writing \(d(A^3) = 3 A^2 dA\). By hand with \(A = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and \(dA = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\): \(A^2 = 0\) so \(3 A^2 dA = 0\), but the product rule gives \(A dA A = A\), which is nonzero.
Forming a vec-Kronecker Jacobian to get a gradient. The differential plus the Frobenius product gives the gradient with no \(n^2 \times n^2\) matrix.
Quoting \(d \log \det X\) without invertibility. The formula needs invertible \(X\); the det gradient \(\det(X)(X^{-1})^\top\) shows the same requirement.

selfTest.q: Derive \(d(X^{-1})\) and name the step where invertibility is used.
selfTest.a: \(XX^{-1} = I\) is constant, so \((dX)X^{-1} + X d(X^{-1}) = 0\) by the product rule. Left-multiplying by \(X^{-1}\) needs \(X\) invertible, giving \(d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1} dX X^{-1}\).

selfTest.q: For \(f(X) = \operatorname{tr}(AXB)\), give \(\operatorname{grad} f\) and the cyclic step.
selfTest.a: \(df = \operatorname{tr}(A dX B) = \operatorname{tr}(BA dX)\) by \(\operatorname{tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{tr}(CAB)\), so \(\operatorname{grad} f = (BA)^\top = A^\top B^\top\) under the Frobenius product.

selfTest.q: Chain \(\mathbb{R}^{100} \to \mathbb{R}^{50} \to \mathbb{R}^{20} \to \mathbb{R}^1\): which accumulation order, with flop counts?
selfTest.a: Left to right (reverse mode). Jacobians are \(1 \times 20\), \(20 \times 50\), \(50 \times 100\): left-to-right costs \(1 \times 20 \times 50 + 1 \times 50 \times 100 = 6000\) multiplications, right-to-left costs \(20 \times 50 \times 100 + 1 \times 20 \times 100 = 102000\). Reverse wins by about 17x.

selfTest.q: Problem Set 1, Problem 2(b)(ii) computes a Jacobian in \(\Theta(n^2)\) given \(A^{-1}\). What is the structural reason?
selfTest.a: With \(M = A + yx^\top\), \(df = -M^{-1} y (dx^\top f)\), so the Jacobian is the rank-1 outer product \(-(M^{-1} y) f(x)^\top\). Sherman-Morrison gives \(M^{-1} v = A^{-1} v - A^{-1} y (x^\top A^{-1} v)/(1 + x^\top A^{-1} y)\), \(\Theta(n^2)\) per vector once \(A^{-1}\) is known, so \(f(x)\), \(M^{-1} y\) and their outer product each cost \(\Theta(n^2)\).

units.title: Gradients of logistic, softmax cross-entropy and regularized losses
outcomes: Derive the logistic sigmoid derivative, the binary-cross-entropy-with-logits gradient \((p - y)x\), and the softmax cross-entropy gradient \(p\) minus one-hot.
Implement the three gradients in NumPy and confirm each against centered differences with a stated tolerance.
Explain why max-subtraction leaves softmax probabilities unchanged and where the naive formula overflows.
units.why: These three gradients are the output layer of almost every classifier you will train. Derive them once and later frameworks only change the packaging.

next.note: That unit fuses log_softmax with max subtraction and uses softmax minus one-hot; this unit derived both.
Stable BCE and the \((p - y)x\) gradient apply this derivation to logistic regression.

study.title: Sigmoid, quadratic and regularizer gradients
study.locator: Exercise 5.2 setup (p. 170): derivative of the logistic sigmoid \(1/(1 + \exp(-x))\). Identities (5.103)-(5.108) (p. 158): \(a^\top X^{-1} b\), \(a^\top Xb\), \(x^\top Bx\) and the weighted least-squares gradient (5.108). Least-squares linear-model pattern (5.75)-(5.78) (p. 154)

study.title: Softmax classifier and numeric stability
study.locator: Softmax classifier section: cross-entropy loss \(L_i = -f_{y_i} + \log \sum_j e^{f_j}\) with the information-theory and MLE views. Practical issues: Numeric stability: max-subtraction trick with the [123, 456, 789] overflow example
study.depth: Read the loss formula and the stability trick only. Derive the gradient yourself in Reproduce; skip the SVM sections and the interactive demo.

focus: \(\operatorname{sigmoid}'(x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(x)(1 - \operatorname{sigmoid}(x))\) falls out of \(\exp' = \exp\); the \((p - y)\) factor comes from \(dL/dp\) cancelling \(dp/ds\).
The softmax cross-entropy gradient is p minus one-hot because the logsumexp derivative is the softmax itself.
\(L_2\) adds \(\lambda w\) under the \((\lambda/2)\|w\|^2\) convention and \(2 \lambda w\) under \(\lambda\|w\|^2\). State the convention before comparing numbers.
Max-subtraction is exact in real arithmetic since it multiplies top and bottom by one constant; it only changes float rounding, which the check measures.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(\operatorname{sigmoid}' = \operatorname{sigmoid}(1 - \operatorname{sigmoid})\), the binary-cross-entropy-with-logits gradient \((p - y)x\), and the softmax cross-entropy gradient \(p - e_y\). Check in float64 NumPy: z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] with y = 0 gives p = [0.659001, 0.242433, 0.098566], loss 0.417030, grad [-0.340999, 0.242433, 0.098566]; max-subtracted softmax agrees with naive to 2.8e-17. A single logistic example (w = [1, 2], x = [0.5, -1], b = 0.5, y = 1) gives p = 0.268941 and dL/dw = [-0.365529, 0.731059].
traps: Averaging versus summing the batch loss changes the gradient by \(1/m\). A mismatched convention looks like a wrong derivation.
Feeding probabilities into a logsumexp. Softmax cross-entropy needs logits; probabilities double-apply the exponential.

Reading softmax outputs as calibrated probabilities. The CS231n notes show that a stronger regularization shrinks the weights and makes the same example's probabilities more diffuse, so only their ordering is meaningful.

selfTest.q: Derive the logistic sigmoid derivative. Which rule and fact?
selfTest.a: \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(x) = (1 + e^{-x})^{-1}\). Chain rule with \(d/dx e^{-x} = -e^{-x}\) gives \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(x)(1 - \operatorname{sigmoid}(x))\).

selfTest.q: One logistic example with \(s = w^\top x + b\) and \(L = -[y \log p + (1 - y) \log(1 - p)]\): show \(dL/dw = (p - y)x\).
selfTest.a: \(dL/dp = (p - y)/(p(1 - p))\) and \(dp/ds = p(1 - p)\), so the product is \(p - y\); times \(ds/dw = x\). The cancellation needs \(p\) strictly inside (0, 1).

selfTest.q: Derive \(dL/dz\) for softmax cross-entropy with true class \(y\).
selfTest.a: \(L = -z_y + \operatorname{logsumexp}(z)\) and \(d/dz_j \operatorname{logsumexp}(z) = p_j\), so the gradient is \(p - e_y\).

selfTest.q: The loss uses \((\lambda/2)\|w\|^2\) in one source and \(\lambda\|w\|^2\) in another. What changes in the gradient?
selfTest.a: \(\lambda w\) versus \(2 \lambda w\). The minimizers agree only after rescaling \(\lambda\), so report the convention with every number.

practice.note: Derive the softmax cross-entropy gradient beside it and check all three gradients with the Reproduce script.

units.stopWhen: Your hand-derived sigmoid, binary-cross-entropy and softmax gradients all match centered differences to 1e-9 relative, and you can state the L2 convention from memory.

units.title: Forward mode, reverse mode, JVPs, VJPs and Hessian-vector products
outcomes: Explain forward mode (JVP) and reverse mode (VJP) and choose between them from input and output counts.
Implement forward-mode dual numbers and a reverse-mode accumulation for a small graph without forming any Jacobian.
Compute a Hessian-vector product by forward-over-reverse or double backward and check it against a finite difference of gradients.
units.why: One reverse pass costs about one forward pass while forward mode costs one pass per input. That cost model decides how every large model is differentiated.

next.note: Dense-layer backprop is reverse mode at scale, and gradient checks test it.
Broadcast backward sums cotangents, which is the VJP of a broadcast; read it as this unit's pullback.

study.title: Forward and reverse-mode automatic differentiation
study.locator: Lecture 5, Part 3 notes (course notes Chapter 8, Sections 8.1 and 8.4): forward mode via dual numbers with the Babylonian square-root example, the cost rule (forward scales with inputs, reverse with outputs) and forward-over-reverse Hessian-vector products (Section 8.4.1)

study.title: Dual numbers and both AD engines
study.locator: Cells Forward mode autodiff using dual numbers (DualNumber class; seeding x gives 24.0 and seeding y gives 10.0 for f at (3, 4)), Reverse mode autodiff (toy engine with backpropagate on the same f), Reverse mode autodiff using PyTorch (torch.autograd.grad with create_graph=True for second order)
study.depth: Rebuild the dual-number and reverse engines independently in your own file; do not copy the notebook cells.

study.title: Backpropagation cost and graph equations
study.locator: Section 5.6 (pp. 159-164): explicit gradient (5.109)-(5.110) motivating the cost worry, forward and backward graph computation with accumulation over parents (5.135)-(5.145), reverse mode cheaper when inputs outnumber labels

study.title: Reverse-mode graph, accumulation and grad modes
study.locator: How autograd encodes the history (reverse-mode graph recording); accumulation into .grad and torch.autograd.grad as a vector-Jacobian product; Grad Modes with Default, No-grad and Inference behavior
study.depth: Consult after your handwritten engine. Skip multithreading and in-place correctness checks.

focus: A JVP pushes a tangent forward (\(Jv\), one column); a VJP pulls a cotangent back (\(v^\top J\), one row). Forward cost scales with \(n\) inputs, reverse with \(m\) outputs.
Reverse mode must keep or recompute forward values. That memory-for-time trade is the price of the single pass.
Dual numbers evaluate \(f(x + \epsilon) = f(x) + f'(x) \epsilon\) exactly since \(\epsilon^2 = 0\); seeding each input in turn gives one gradient column per pass.
An HVP is the JVP of the gradient. It needs \(C^2\) so the differentiation order does not matter.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement a minimal DualNumber type (\(\epsilon^2 = 0\)) and recover \(df/dx = 24.0\) and \(df/dy = 10.0\) for \(f(x, y) = x^2 y + y + 2\) at (3, 4), matching the notebook analytic values. State the cost rule: \(n\) inputs with 1 output take 1 reverse pass versus \(n\) forward passes. Verify an HVP without forming \(H\) on \(f(x) = 0.5 x^\top Ax + b^\top x\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with \(A = M + M^\top + 3I\), drawing \(M\) (\(3 \times 3\)), \(b\), \(x\) and \(v\) in that order with standard_normal from numpy.random.default_rng(11) in float64: the centered difference \((\operatorname{grad} f(x + hv) - \operatorname{grad} f(x - hv))/(2h)\) at \(h = 10^{-5}\) misses \(Av\) by 2.2e-11 in the 2-norm. The gradient is linear, so that gap is rounding alone.
traps: Building the full Jacobian to get one JVP or VJP. Propagate the vector instead; the matrix is never needed.
Calling torch.autograd.functional.jacobian for a check on wide maps. It materializes the matrix; use grad (a VJP) or directional differences.
Assuming reverse mode always wins. For \(\mathbb{R}^1 \to \mathbb{R}^N\), one forward pass beats \(N\) reverse passes, so count outputs before choosing.

selfTest.q: Compare forward and reverse cost for \(f: \mathbb{R}^{1000} \to \mathbb{R}\).
selfTest.a: Reverse costs about one forward pass; forward costs about 1000 passes, one per input. Uses: each primitive JVP or VJP costs \(O(1)\) forward equivalents.

selfTest.q: What do a JVP and a VJP compute, and which one does torch.autograd.grad perform?
selfTest.a: JVP computes \(Jv\) (pushforward of a tangent); VJP computes \(v^\top J\) (pullback of a cotangent). torch.autograd.grad performs a VJP.

selfTest.q: Give the two HVP routes and the assumption each needs.
selfTest.a: Forward-over-reverse (JVP of the gradient) or double backward (VJP of the gradient). Both need \(C^2\) so mixed partials agree and the order is irrelevant.

selfTest.q: Why does reverse mode store forward values?
selfTest.a: Local pullbacks need operand values (for example d(a*b) needs a and b). The forward pass saves them; recomputation trades time for memory.

units.title: Backpropagation through dense layers and gradient checks
outcomes: Derive backprop through an affine map, an elementwise nonlinearity and a branched sum, with shapes stated.
Implement centered-difference gradient checks including random-direction tests for matrix parameters, with tolerance and norm stated.
Diagnose step-size, cancellation, nondifferentiability and stochastic-state failures from the error curve.
units.why: Backprop hides a sign, transpose or accumulation bug in every new layer. A two-evaluation directional check finds it in seconds; a per-coordinate loop costs \(2mn\) evaluations.

next.note: That unit standardizes centered differences in float64 with \(h = 10^{-5}\) and relative error; this unit's directional test is its matrix-valued companion.
Use these checks to validate the scalar engine against centered differences.

study.locator: Lecture 5, Part 3 notes (course notes Chapter 8, Section 8.3): computational graphs, summing products along every input-to-output path, and reverse mode on graphs (Section 8.3.1)

focus: Centered differences carry \(O(h^2)\) error until rounding at about \(\epsilon/h\) takes over; \(h = 10^{-5}\) in float64 sits near the bottom of that U-curve.
The random-direction test \(\langle G, V \rangle\) against the directional difference needs 2 evaluations for any shape and catches transpose and scale bugs. Use several seeded \(V\).
Backprop through a branch sums cotangents from every downstream use. A missing accumulation is the classic silent bug.
Relative error needs a scale: use \(\|num - ana\| / (\|num\| + \|ana\|)\) so near-zero gradients do not explode the ratio.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, backpropagate \(L = 0.5\|\tanh(Wx + b) - t\|^2\) with \(W\) (\(2 \times 3\)), \(b\) (\(2\)), \(x\) (\(3\)), \(t\) (\(2\)) and direction \(V\) (\(2 \times 3\)) drawn in that order with standard_normal from numpy.random.default_rng(5) in float64: \(\delta = (a - t) .* (1 - a^2)\), \(dL/dW = \delta x^\top\). Measured: \(L\) = 1.73395370, centered differences (\(h = 10^{-5}\)) give relative error \(\|num - ana\|/(\|num\| + \|ana\|)\) = 3.4e-11, and the direction test \(|\langle dW, V \rangle - (L(W + hV) - L(W - hV))/(2h)|\) = 1.4e-10. Repeat at \(h = 0.1\) to get relative error 4.3e-3, consistent with \(O(h^2)\) truncation.
traps: Checking at one h far from 1e-5 without a sweep. For the tanh layer in Reproduce, h = 0.1 leaves 4.3e-3 relative error and hides real bugs above the truncation floor, while h = 1e-12 drowns in cancellation.
Gradchecking through a kink or a stochastic op and reading the mismatch as a backprop bug. Freeze stochasticity and keep nondifferentiable points out of the check.
Comparing with == or to too many digits. State the norm and tolerance; for the tanh layer, float64 centered differences bottom out near 1e-10, not 1e-16.

selfTest.q: Write the backward pass for \(z = Wx + b\), \(a = \tanh(z)\), \(L = 0.5\|a - t\|^2\), with shapes.
selfTest.a: \(\delta = (a - t) .* (1 - a^2)\), shape \(m\). \(dL/dW = \delta x^\top\) (\(m \times n\)), \(dL/db = \delta\), \(dL/dx = W^\top \delta\). The outer product, not an inner product, gives \(m \times n\).

selfTest.q: Why is centered \(O(h^2)\) while one-sided is \(O(h)\)?
selfTest.a: Taylor expansion: the forward difference leaves a first-order term \(f''h/2\), while centering cancels all odd powers of \(h\), leaving \(O(h^2)\). The remainder form needs \(C^3\).

selfTest.q: \(W\) has 6 entries. Compare per-coordinate and directional check cost.
selfTest.a: Per-coordinate costs 12 evaluations; one direction costs 2. Run 3 to 5 random directions from a seeded generator and record the seed, dtype and norm.

selfTest.q: The check disagrees only at entries whose pre-activation sits near zero under ReLU. Is backprop wrong?
selfTest.a: Probably not. Centered differences average left and right slopes at a nondifferentiable kink. Move the check point or use a smooth activation for the check.
